description: We are a passionate team interested in space technology, AI, and data science. Our goal is to build innovative, data-driven solutions using NASA’s open data. We welcome motivated teammates skilled in AI/ML, Python, web development, and data visualization who want to collaborate and make a real impact.
summary:
EarthTrend Explorer is an interactive climate data analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the challenge “Be An Earth System Trend Detective.”

The platform combines NASA GISTEMP global temperature records with Rutgers University’s Northern Hemisphere snow cover data to explore long-term changes in Earth's climate system. It provides interactive visualizations, annual and seasonal trend analysis, statistical methods such as linear regression, Mann-Kendall testing and Sen’s slope, and cross-variable correlation analysis using Pearson and Spearman coefficients. Users can compare aligned datasets, explore climate patterns, identify significant trends, and download analysis results as CSV files.

EarthTrend Explorer addresses the challenge by transforming complex environmental datasets into accessible, interpretable insights. It helps students, researchers, and climate enthusiasts explore relationships between climate indicators and better understand long-term environmental changes. By making scientific data easier to analyze and communicate, the platform encourages data-driven climate awareness and exploration.
details:
Project Details – EarthTrend Explorer

EarthTrend Explorer is an interactive web-based platform designed to help users investigate long-term changes in Earth's climate system through scientific data analysis and visualization.

The project combines NASA GISTEMP global temperature anomaly data with Northern Hemisphere snow cover data from Rutgers Global Snow Lab. Users can explore annual temperature changes, seasonal patterns, snow cover trends, and relationships between these climate indicators through interactive charts and visualizations.

The platform uses statistical techniques such as Linear Regression, Mann-Kendall Trend Testing, Sen's Slope, Pearson Correlation, and Spearman Correlation to identify trends and examine relationships between datasets. It also provides statistical summaries, rolling averages, and CSV export functionality so users can explore and reuse the analysis results.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
EarthTrend Explorer makes complex climate datasets easier to understand and explore. It supports students, educators, researchers, and climate enthusiasts in identifying environmental patterns and developing a better understanding of long-term climate changes. Its intended impact is to encourage scientific curiosity, climate awareness, and data-driven exploration of Earth's changing environment.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Frontend: React.js
  • Programming Language: JavaScript
  • Build Tool: Vite
  • Web Technologies: HTML and CSS
  • Data Sources: NASA GISTEMP and Rutgers Global Snow Lab
  • Statistical Analysis: Custom JavaScript implementations of statistical methods
  • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code
  • Version Control and Code Hosting: Git and GitHub

Creativity and Innovation:
The project's creative approach is to bring multiple climate indicators together in one interactive platform instead of presenting them as separate datasets. It combines visual exploration with statistical analysis, allowing users to investigate both individual trends and cross-variable relationships. The use of normalized comparisons, multiple statistical methods, and downloadable results makes climate data exploration more accessible and informative.

Factors Considered During Development:
Our team considered data reliability, scientific accuracy, missing or incomplete observations, differences in dataset coverage, statistical limitations, ease of use, and performance. We also ensured that incomplete annual observations were not incorrectly treated as complete data and that correlation results were interpreted as statistical relationships rather than proof of causation.
